title: A stretched rubber band shrinks when you heat it
body: Most things expand when warmed, but hold a rubber band under tension, warm it with a hair dryer, and it pulls tighter. Rubber is made of long tangled chains that are constantly jostled by heat. Stretching straightens them, which cuts the number of ways they can arrange themselves, a drop in what physicists call **entropy**. The warmer the rubber, the harder the chains fight to re-tangle, so the band contracts. The flip side is easy to feel: stretch a band quickly against your lip and it warms; let it snap back and it cools.

slides.alt: Two panels. Left, a relaxed rubber band with tangled polymer chains inside, labelled many arrangements. Right, a stretched band with nearly straight chains, labelled few arrangements. Arrows show pulling and heating.
slides.caption: Stretching straightens the chains; heat makes them want to tangle again.

steps.label: Stretch a thick band fast: it feels warm
Hold it: it cools back to room temperature
Let it snap back: it feels cool

events.text: John Gough publishes the first observations of rubber warming when stretched
James Joule measures the heating carefully, confirming Lord Kelvin’s prediction

left.label: Sounds like
left.text: Rubber has ‘negative thermal expansion’ and shrinks whenever it is heated.

right.label: Actually
right.text: An unstretched band expands when warmed, like almost everything. The shrinking only shows up while the band is held under tension.

slides.question: Why does a stretched rubber band pull tighter when warmed?
slides.explanation: Heat jostles the long chains harder, and tangled chains have far more possible arrangements than straight ones, so the band pulls itself shorter.

slides.clue: The physicists’ count of possible arrangements, which drops when you straighten rubber’s chains
slides.detail: Heat drives the chains back toward their many tangled arrangements, so a warm band held under tension pulls itself shorter.
